title: The Art of Asking Good Questions
paragraphs: Asking a good question is a skill. It sounds obvious, but most people — including many university students — have never been explicitly taught how to do it. They ask questions that are too vague, too leading, or simply unclear. They interrupt before the other person has finished answering. They ask several questions at once, leaving the person they're asking unsure which to address first. The result is usually a poor answer, not because the other person doesn't know, but because the question didn't give them enough direction.

At WKU, Professor Aidarov has started something new: a "Question of the Week" session at the start of each Thursday lecture. Before the session, students must submit one question they genuinely want answered — about the topic, about language learning, about career paths, about anything academically relevant. The constraint: the question must be written as a proper indirect question. Not "Where is the stress in English?" but "Could you explain where the stress tends to fall in English compound nouns?"

The difference, Professor Aidarov explains, is significant. A direct question can feel abrupt or even aggressive in a formal context. "When you ask 'Where is the stress?'" he says, "you sound like you're demanding information. When you ask 'Could you tell me where the stress falls?' you sound like you're requesting it. The same information. Completely different relationship."

Students have responded enthusiastically. Kamila says the exercise has changed how she asks questions in seminars and even in everyday conversation. "I used to fire off questions like machine gun bullets," she admits. "Now I think before I ask. I consider what I actually want to know, how specific my question needs to be, and whether I'm asking the right person at the right moment."

Amir agrees, though he approaches the skill from a different angle. "In computer science, the way you phrase a question to a search engine or an AI tool determines everything about the quality of the answer you get," he says. "Garbage in, garbage out. The same is true for human conversations. If I ask my supervisor a poorly structured question, I get a vague answer. If I ask a precise, well-framed question, I get exactly what I need."

Rustam, characteristically, offers a simpler observation. "The best question is the one that makes the other person think," he says. "Not the one that traps them. Not the one that shows off what you already know. The one that actually opens something up." He pauses. "I also think there's a lot to be said for not asking anything and just listening carefully. You learn a lot more than you think."

Tag questions are another important tool. "You've been to Almaty, haven't you?" invites confirmation and conversation. "It's a beautiful city, isn't it?" checks that the listener shares your view. These small additions to statements — the tags — keep conversation alive. They signal openness. They say: "I'm not just talking at you. I want to know what you think too."

The ability to ask clearly, listen actively, and follow up precisely is one of the most valuable communication skills a student can develop. It is also, perhaps, one of the most underrated. Universities teach students what to know. They rarely teach them how to ask.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: Could you tell me what "indirect questions" means exactly? I keep confusing them with reported speech.

dialogue.speaker: Aidarov
dialogue.text: Good question — and perfectly phrased as an indirect question, incidentally. Indirect questions are polite question forms embedded in a larger structure.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: Could you give me an example?

dialogue.speaker: Aidarov
dialogue.text: "Where is the library?" becomes "Could you tell me where the library is?" Notice the word order changes.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: Ah — so the verb stays after the subject. It doesn't invert like in a direct question.

dialogue.speaker: Aidarov
dialogue.text: Exactly. "Do you know what time the lecture starts?" — not "Do you know what time does the lecture start?"

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: And tag questions? Could you tell me when we use those?

dialogue.speaker: Aidarov
dialogue.text: Tags are added to the end of statements to check information or invite agreement. "You're a linguist, aren't you?" — you already believe it; you're confirming.
